new_settlements.name: Bekir Pasha Aqueduct (Kamares)
new_settlements.modern: Western edge of Larnaca, Larnaca district
new_settlements.desc: The largest public work of Ottoman Cyprus, built from 1747 by Ebubekir Pasha, briefly governor of the island, to bring water about ten kilometres from the Tremithos valley at Arpera to the growing port of Larnaca, which until then depended on brackish wells. Water moved entirely by gravity through a buried channel punctuated by some 250 shafts, surfacing in three arcaded spans of which seventy-five arches survive. It supplied the town until 1939 and was repaired in 1854 and again in 1876 at the expense of the pious foundation Ebubekir had endowed. It is the standing argument against the view that the Ottoman centuries built nothing on Cyprus.

finds.t: The best-preserved arcade, a run of pointed limestone arches carrying the channel across the flood plain of a seasonal river; the name Kamares simply means 'the arches'. It is floodlit at night and is the emblem of modern Larnaca.

finds.n: The buried conduit and its air shafts
finds.t: Between the visible spans the water ran in a covered masonry channel tapped by roughly 250 shafts, a qanat technique of Persian ancestry used across the Ottoman world. The shafts let workmen in to clear silt and kept the head of water falling at a constant, very shallow gradient.
finds.w: In situ, between Arpera and Larnaca

finds.t: The upstream works in the Tremithos valley, on land held as a farm estate of the governor, where springs and river water were gathered into the channel. Much of the intake is now hard to trace on the ground.
finds.w: In situ, near Arpera, Larnaca district

finds.n: The waqf endowment of Ebubekir Pasha
finds.t: The aqueduct was given to a charitable foundation whose rents paid for its upkeep and for public fountains in Larnaca, which is why repairs were still being made in 1854 and 1876 long after its builder had gone. Ottoman public works on Cyprus were funded this way rather than from a provincial budget.
The aqueduct fed public fountains in the town and in the consular quarter of Skala, several of which survive as reused stone basins and wall spouts. Piped water replaced the whole system in 1939.

A five-year conservation programme on one of the spans began in 1987, and the monument is now a protected ancient monument in a public park. Some of the mortar repairs of the 1980s are themselves now criticised as too hard for the original limestone.

new_settlements.name: Peristerona
new_settlements.modern: Peristerona, Nicosia district, on the Serrachis
new_settlements.desc: A mixed village on the Serrachis river whose church and mosque stand a few dozen metres apart, an image that appeared on Cypriot banknotes and stamps as the emblem of the two communities living together. The church of Saints Barnabas and Hilarion is one of only two five-domed churches on the island, built in the ninth or tenth century, and the Ottoman mosque beside it served a Turkish Cypriot population that lived in Peristerona until 1964. The village is on Cyprus's UNESCO tentative list. The pairing is now read very differently by the two communities, and the mosque stands without a congregation.

finds.n: Church of Saints Barnabas and Hilarion
finds.t: A cross-in-square church carrying five domes in a quincunx, the only such plan on Cyprus apart from Agia Paraskevi at Geroskipou. Part of the north wall of a still earlier church survives inside the west wall.

The oldest surviving painting in the church is fifteenth and sixteenth century, later than the building itself; the carved and gilded iconostasis and its icons are post-Byzantine work of the Ottoman centuries.

A plain rectangular prayer hall with a stubby minaret standing on the same river terrace as the church. Its exact date is not securely published; the building as it stands looks eighteenth or nineteenth century.

finds.n: The church and mosque on the currency
finds.t: The two buildings photographed together were used by the Republic on banknotes, stamps and tourist posters as an official image of coexistence, which makes the picture a historical document about the 1960s as much as about the buildings.
finds.w: Central Bank of Cyprus collection; Cyprus Post archives

finds.n: The medieval bridge over the Serrachis
finds.p: Medieval, repaired in the Ottoman period
finds.t: A stone bridge on the old Nicosia to Morphou road that made the village a crossing point and a stopping place for caravans; the modern road now bypasses it.

Peristerona's Turkish Cypriot inhabitants left during the intercommunal fighting of 1963 to 1964 and did not return; their houses were later occupied or fell in. The village is one of the clearest places to see what the unmixing of the island's villages looked like on the ground.

Three domes run down the central aisle with one over each side aisle, so that from outside the roof reads as a cross. The idea is generally traced to Justinian's church of St John at Ephesus and the Holy Apostles in Constantinople, both now gone.

There is no foundation inscription and no early document, so the church is dated on its architecture alone; estimates run from the tenth century to the early twelfth, and its relationship to Geroskipou, usually placed a century earlier, is unsettled.
Only patches survive on the thick internal walls, far less than at the Troodos churches, which is one reason Peristerona is less visited than its architecture deserves.
A carved and gilded screen carrying icons of the sixteenth century and after, including a well-known pair of the church's two patron saints.

An Ottoman mosque stands within a few metres of the church across the riverbed. The pairing was photographed endlessly under British rule and printed on stamps as proof that the two communities could live side by side.

new_settlements.name: Chrysorrogiatissa Monastery
new_settlements.desc: A monastery on a ridge above the Paphos forest, founded by tradition in 1152 by a hermit named Ignatios who found an icon of the Virgin washed up on the coast at Moulia. Everything now standing was rebuilt from 1770 under Abbot Ioakim, in the burst of monastic building that followed the loosening of Ottoman controls on the Church, and its cliffside courtyard and winery show what a working Cypriot monastery of the late Ottoman period looked like. It ran one of the island's few libraries and printing interests, and it still makes wine from its own vines.

finds.t: A single-aisled church raised on the footings of an older one by Abbot Ioakim, with a carved and gilded iconostasis and a barrel vault; the surrounding two-storey ranges with their wooden verandas were built at the same time.

finds.p: Traditionally 1st century; the visible panel is later
finds.t: A silver-clad icon of the Virgin ascribed by tradition to Saint Luke and said to have been thrown into the sea in Asia Minor during the iconoclast persecution. As with the Kykkos icon, the painting itself cannot be seen under its revetment and the tradition is devotional rather than art-historical.

Vaulted cellars where the monks pressed and stored wine; commercial winemaking was restarted in the 1980s and the monastery bottles under its own label. Monastic viticulture is the thread that connects Commandaria, the Ottoman-era village wine trade and the modern Cypriot industry.

finds.n: Icons and manuscripts of the monastery museum
finds.t: Post-Byzantine icons, embroidered vestments, printed books and manuscripts, the working library of a monastery that also acted as a school and a bank for the villages around it.

finds.n: The Byzantine museum collection from the Paphos hills
finds.t: Icons gathered from the small churches of the district and displayed at the monastery, including panels stripped from chapels that could no longer be guarded. The concentration of icons in monasteries is a response to the thefts of the 1970s and 1980s as much as to piety.

finds.n: The grave of Makarios's home village
finds.t: Pano Panagia below the monastery is the birthplace of Archbishop Makarios III, and his family house is a museum; the monastery is part of the landscape that produced the first president of the Republic.
A three-sided range around a court with wooden galleries and a small domed church, the standard plan of a post-Byzantine Cypriot monastery, replacing whatever the medieval house had.
Panels, gospel books and vestments in the monastery museum, including work of the Italo-Byzantine manner that spread through Cyprus in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

The monastery's own vineyards and cellar, working again on a commercial basis; monastic wine-making on Cyprus is continuous from the period when Commandaria and Cypriot muscat were shipped to western courts.
The abbot was among the churchmen killed in the Ottoman reprisals of July 1821, the violent end of the arrangement by which the Orthodox hierarchy had governed the Greek population since 1571.

new_settlements.name: Fikardou
new_settlements.desc: A mountain village at 900 metres that lost its people rather than its houses, and so preserves the vernacular architecture of Ottoman Cyprus almost complete: stone walls, timber-framed upper storeys, hooked roof tiles and cobbled lanes. It was declared an ancient monument in 1978 and won a Europa Nostra award in 1987, and two of its houses are now museums of rural life. Fikardou shows what the villages that produced the island's wine, silk and grain actually looked like, which no palace or mosque can.

finds.t: The finest surviving house in the village, with a stone-carved twin-arched window, a steep pitched roof of hooked tiles and a first-floor living room reached by an outside stair. Owned by the Department of Antiquities and shown as a museum.

The second museum house, with its wine press, storage jars and looms in place, forming with Katsinioros the village's rural museum. The two together show the ground floor as workshop and the upper floor as home.

finds.n: Wine presses and buried storage jars
finds.t: Stone treading floors and sunken pithoi for must, the equipment of a village whose cash crop was wine sold down to the towns; the Pitsilia villages supplied both the local trade and the zivania stills.

Walls of local stone laid in mud mortar with timber lacing, and floors of beaten earth over reeds and beams, a system that needs constant maintenance; the restoration deliberately used the same materials rather than cement.

finds.n: Church of the Apostles Peter and Paul
finds.t: The village church, small and low with a carved iconostasis, whose parish records track the emptying of the village through the twentieth century.

The whole village, not a single building, was scheduled as an ancient monument, an unusual step on Cyprus and the reason Fikardou was not rebuilt in concrete. Its permanent population is now in single figures.

new_settlements.name: Pano Lefkara
new_settlements.desc: A hill town on the southern slopes of the Troodos that made its living from needlework and silver rather than from land. Its drawn-thread embroidery, lefkaritika, mixes local white-work with Venetian cut-work patterns, and from the late nineteenth century Lefkara men carried it by ship to Europe and even to Scandinavia and America while the women made it at home. UNESCO added the craft to its intangible heritage list in 2009. In the sixteenth century Lefkara was reckoned among the largest places on the island and it was a fief in the Ottoman period; its population is now under a thousand.

finds.p: From at least the 14th century; codified 19th century
finds.t: Cut and drawn linen worked in hemstitch and satin filling in white, ecru and brown, built from a fixed vocabulary of geometric motifs with names such as the river and the mill wheel. The debt to sixteenth-century Italian punto tagliato is visible and undisputed; the Leonardo da Vinci story is not.
finds.w: In situ; Museum of Traditional Embroidery and Silversmithing, Pano Lefkara

finds.t: The town's best-known story has Leonardo da Vinci calling at Cyprus and carrying a Lefkara altar cloth back to Milan cathedral. There is no documentary support for it and Leonardo's Cypriot visit is itself unevidenced, but the tale has been repeated since the nineteenth century and is now part of the craft's marketing.

A school opened in the village to teach and standardise the work, part of a late Ottoman and early British effort to turn a dowry craft into an export industry. The travelling salesmen, kentitarides, and the home embroiderers, ploumarisses, were the two halves of the trade.

Filigree in silver wire, made for church use and for jewellery, worked in the same houses as the embroidery and sold by the same travellers. The craft survives in a handful of workshops on the main street.
finds.w: In situ; Museum of Traditional Embroidery and Silversmithing

finds.t: The town's principal church, holding a silver-gilt reliquary cross said to contain a fragment of the True Cross brought by Saint Helena, and a collection of icons; its treasury reflects the wealth the embroidery trade brought back.

Narrow shaded lanes of two-storey houses with bare stone facades, few openings and flat rammed-earth roofs, a building type adapted to heat and to a town where work was done indoors. Much of it was restored rather than replaced once tourism arrived in the 1970s.

Lefkara laces were inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009, Cyprus's first such listing, in part because the number of working embroiderers was falling fast.
finds.w: UNESCO; Department of Modern Cultural Heritage, Cyprus

new_settlements.name: Troodos hill station and the summer capital
new_settlements.desc: Within a year of taking over the island the British began building a summer residence for the High Commissioner high on the Troodos, and the government followed it up the mountain every summer for the rest of the colonial period. It was a hill station in the Indian manner, with a military camp, a police post, tennis courts and a hotel, and it made the mountain forest a place of government as well as of monasteries. The residence is still the Cypriot president's summer house, and the surrounding forest became the island's first national forest park.

finds.t: A stone and timber house begun under Lieutenant George Wisely of the Royal Engineers at the prompting of the second High Commissioner, Sir Robert Biddulph, who wanted to escape Nicosia's summer. Modernised under President Clerides between 1999 and 2001 and still the presidential summer residence.

Arthur Rimbaud worked in Cyprus in 1879 to 1881 and by local tradition served as foreman on the governor's cottage; his own letters place him at a quarry and on building work on the island, but scholars regard the specific link to this house as unproven. A plaque on the mountain commemorates it anyway.

A summer camp for the garrison beside the residence, later used as a training and rest station and during the 1955 to 1959 emergency as a base for operations in the mountains. Parts are still in military use.

finds.n: The Troodos road and the mule track
finds.t: Getting the summer government up the mountain meant a carriage road from Nicosia through Kakopetria, one of the first big British public works, replacing mule tracks. Road building was the most visible achievement of the early administration and also its biggest expense.

The forest around the summit, protected in the colonial period as state forest against goats and charcoal burners, is now a national forest park with a visitor centre, and the source of much of the island's water.

finds.n: The Berengaria and the mountain hotels
finds.t: Prodromos and Platres below the summit filled with summer hotels for Cypriots, Egyptians and Levantines escaping the heat; the ruined Berengaria at Prodromos is the most photographed relic of that trade.
finds.w: In situ, Prodromos and Pano Platres

new_settlements.name: Cyprus Government Railway, Evrychou terminus
new_settlements.desc: The mountain end of the island's only public railway, a 762 mm narrow-gauge line that ran 122 km from Famagusta harbour through Nicosia to Morphou and finally, from 1915, to Evrychou at the foot of the Troodos. It was built to carry carobs, grain and copper to the port and never made a profit; buses and lorries killed it and the last train ran on 31 December 1951. Evrychou's station survived as a warehouse and reopened as the Cyprus Railway Museum in November 2014, which is the best place to see what the line was.

finds.t: A single-storey stone station with its platform, office and goods shed, the terminus of Section 3 from Morphou; restored and opened as the Cyprus Railway Museum in November 2014.

One of the line's twelve locomotives, from Hunslet of Leeds, preserved as a monument at Famagusta station. The stock also included Nasmyth Wilson and Kitson engines, all tiny by British standards because of the narrow gauge.

Famagusta to Nicosia, 58 km, opened 21 October 1905; Nicosia to Morphou, 39 km, in 1907; Morphou to Evrychou, 24 km, in 1915. Thirty-nine stations, stops and halts served a population that mostly walked.
A separate mineral line ran from the Skouriotissa and Mavrovouni mines to the company pier at Xeros and kept working until 1974, outliving the government railway by more than twenty years.
finds.w: Trackbed in situ, Skouriotissa to Karavostasi

finds.n: The Kaimakli and Ayios Dometios linear parks
finds.t: Two stretches of the Nicosia trackbed have been turned into linear parks with restored rail and a station platform, the easiest place in the capital to stand on the old line.

The railway closed as a deliberate act of policy after decades of losses and competition from the improved road network; the rails were lifted and sold, which is why so little survives beyond stations and embankments.

new_settlements.name: Skouriotissa
new_settlements.modern: Skouriotissa, Nicosia district, and Mavrovouni across the ceasefire line
new_settlements.desc: The island's copper came back to life here in the twentieth century, on ground already worked in antiquity and buried under ancient slag; the village name means 'Our Lady of the Slag'. The Cyprus Mines Corporation, founded in 1916 by the American Mudd family after Charles Gunther's prospecting from 1914, reopened Skouriotissa and then the far richer Mavrovouni orebody in 1929, built a company town and a pier at Xeros and made copper and pyrite the colony's largest export and largest private employer. Long strikes in 1948 organised by the Pancyprian Federation of Labour marked the birth of modern Cypriot trade unionism. In 1974 the ceasefire line cut the mines from their processing plant and the company left the island; Skouriotissa is again producing copper today.

finds.t: Hundreds of thousands of tonnes of black smelting slag lie around the mine, the residue of Hellenistic and Roman workings; the modern company found ancient galleries, wooden tools and Roman coins as it cut into the hill. The slag itself was later reprocessed.
A massive sulphide orebody north-west of Skouriotissa, the richest the company worked; after 1974 it lay on the far side of the ceasefire line from the mill and has not been worked since.
finds.w: In situ, north of the ceasefire line

finds.n: The company town and pier at Xeros
finds.t: American-planned housing, a hospital, a school and a club at Xeros and Karavostasi, with an ore pier and a narrow-gauge line down from the mines; the town's segregation of staff and labour housing was as characteristic as its welfare provision.

The pits now worked at Skouriotissa, where low-grade ore is heap-leached and copper is won by electrowinning as cathode sheets rather than smelted, which is why the mine can claim to be among the longest-worked copper sites in the world.

A long stoppage in the mines, led by the left-wing Pancyprian Federation of Labour; the government declined to intervene on the ground that wages were not substandard. The mining villages became the core of the Cypriot left.
The small church that gave the place its name, once the seat of a monastery among the slag heaps; it was left inside the buffer zone after 1974 and is reached only with UN permission.
The near-abandoned village, with eight residents at the 2001 census, now houses the headquarters of the Argentine-led sector of the United Nations force, a mining settlement turned peacekeeping base.

Great banks of black smelting waste, still carrying traces of residual copper, spread across the district and protected as monuments. They are the largest visible remains of the industry that made ancient Cyprus rich.

Galleries and shafts driven into the ore body when surface deposits ran out, the earliest underground mining on the island. Roman activity here is well attested but the workings themselves have never been systematically excavated or dated.

Roman slag has been found as much as 3 km from the workings that produced the ore, meaning the rock was carried to the fuel rather than fuel to the rock. That is a reversal of Bronze Age practice and a sign of how far the woodland had been cut back.
finds.w: In situ, various sites in the Troodos foothills

finds.n: The imperial mines and Herod's lease
finds.t: Under Rome the mines were held directly by the emperor and worked by contract; Josephus records Augustus handing Herod half the revenue and the lease of the rest. Only Amathus, Tamassos and Soli are named as still producing under Rome, a much smaller industry than in the Bronze Age.

The Cyprus Mines Corporation was founded on the strength of the Roman tailings, which told Gunther where to dig. Modern Cypriot mining and much of the island's twentieth-century economy grew from an archaeological observation.

new_settlements.name: Amiantos asbestos mine
new_settlements.desc: The largest asbestos mine in Europe, cut into the serpentine of the Troodos above 1,100 metres. Working began in 1904 when an Italian bought the licence from the British administration, and over the life of the mine roughly 130 million tonnes of rock were moved to win about a million tonnes of chrysotile fibre from ore grading barely one per cent. It closed in 1988, leaving a grey scar visible from the far side of the island and a legacy of asbestos disease among its workers. Rehabilitation began in 1995 and is expected to run to 2030; it is the largest environmental restoration project on Cyprus.

finds.t: Terraced benches and waste dumps covering about 4.7 square kilometres, the shape of an industry that had to move a hundred tonnes of rock for each tonne of fibre. The mine is fenced but visible from the Troodos road.
Crushing and fibre-separation sheds, conveyors and the company offices, some restored as part of the rehabilitation and interpreted for visitors, others left as ruins.
Pano Amiantos grew as a company settlement of workers' housing, shops and a school at an altitude where nobody would otherwise have lived, and shrank when the mine closed.

Cypriot cohorts of former Amiantos workers have been studied for asbestosis and mesothelioma; the long latency means cases were still appearing decades after the mine shut. Dust control at the mine was poor for most of its life.
finds.w: Medical literature; Ministry of Health, Cyprus

finds.t: Slopes were reshaped and stabilised, soil manufactured from waste and compost, and native Troodos species hydroseeded and planted; the work has been part-funded through the European Economic Area grants and is a reference case for mine restoration on serpentine soils.

A botanical garden laid out on reclaimed mine ground, planted with the endemic flora of the Troodos massif, with an environmental information centre; the endemics of the ophiolite are the reason the restoration could not simply plant pines.

new_settlements.name: The barn at Liopetri (Achyronas)
new_settlements.desc: A straw barn on the edge of a Kokkinochoria village where four EOKA fighters were surrounded by British troops on 2 September 1958 and killed after a battle of about five hours, having refused to surrender. The fight became the best-known set-piece of the emergency after the death of Afxentiou, and Grivas ended the truce he had declared in August in response. The barn was preserved as a national memorial and a bronze group of the four men was unveiled on 7 September 1997.

finds.t: A low mud-brick and stone straw store, kept as it was with its bullet damage, now roofed and enclosed as a memorial museum. Its ordinariness is the point: the emergency was fought in farmyards.
Andreas Karyos, Christos Samaras, Ilias Papakyriakou and Fotis Pittas, all local men, died in the barn; a British soldier was also killed. Their names are on the monument and on the village school.
A group of four figures beside the barn, one of the most visited EOKA memorials in the island's south-east; the anniversary is marked every September.
Army and police reports of the cordon and the five-hour fire fight, including the decision to burn the barn out, are in the British archives and are the main non-Cypriot account of the action.
Grivas had suspended operations in August while the Macmillan plan was discussed; the Liopetri deaths ended the pause, a reminder of how closely the fighting tracked the negotiations in London.
The village around the barn is a Kokkinochoria farming settlement, its red soil under potatoes; the four men were farmers, and the barn held that year's straw.

new_settlements.name: Machairas Monastery
new_settlements.desc: A stavropegic monastery at about 870 m on the north flank of the Machairas range, founded by the hermits Neophytos and Ignatios who, tradition says, found an icon of the Virgin in a cave in 1145 and had to cut their way to it with a knife, machaira, which gave the house its name. Ignatios went to Constantinople in 1172 and came back with the endowment of Manuel I Komnenos, the whole mountain and independence from the local bishop. The monk Neilos enlarged it in the early thirteenth century and wrote its typikon. It burned in 1892 and everything standing is later, but it is the best surviving example of a great Byzantine foundation that kept its independence through three centuries of Latin rule.

finds.t: A dugout in the hillside below the monastery, marked by a memorial and a bronze eagle, where Afxentiou held out for about ten hours after his four companions surrendered. The Royal Engineers poured petrol down the slope and set it alight.
The katholikon holds the icon of the Panagia Machairiotissa, said to have been found in a cave reached by cutting through scrub with a knife, machairi, which gave the house its name.

Fire destroyed much of the monastery in 1892; the archimandrite Chariton raised 6,483 roubles in the Russian Empire towards rebuilding, one of many links between Cypriot monasteries and Russian patronage in the late Ottoman and early British years.

A small museum at the monastery holding his belongings, photographs and documents of the campaign, kept by the monks; Afxentiou himself is buried at the Imprisoned Graves in Nicosia, where the British put him.

finds.n: The monastery forest as EOKA ground
finds.t: The Machairas and Kykkos forests gave cover for mountain groups, arms caches and printing; the British response was cordon and search operations that swept whole valleys, and the monasteries were repeatedly raided.
The archbishop, who had been abbot of Machairas, was buried here in 2022, an unusual choice that ties the modern Church back to the mountain houses.
The cave icon that gave the monastery its name, silver-cased and credited to Saint Luke like the Kykkos panel; the tradition of an Asia Minor origin fits the iconoclast-era flight of icons to Cyprus.
The monastery's rule, written by its first abbot, one of the few Cypriot monastic charters to survive and a detailed source on landholding, serf labour and diet in the first Lusignan generation.

The imperial grant of the mountain and of stavropegic status, meaning the house answered to Constantinople and not to the bishop; after 1260 that independence was what let it survive under a Latin hierarchy.
finds.w: Documentary; recorded in the monastery's archive

finds.t: The EOKA commander Grigoris Afxentiou was burned out of a dugout below the monastery on 3 March 1957; the hideout and a museum are now part of any visit.
Machairas held villages, vineyards and mills across the eastern Troodos, and its tenants paid in wine and silk; Orthodox houses like this kept a Greek landholding class alive under Frankish lordship.

new_settlements.name: Akrotiri and the Sovereign Base Areas
new_settlements.modern: Akrotiri peninsula, and Dhekelia in the east
new_settlements.desc: When Cyprus became independent in 1960 Britain kept 254 square kilometres, about three per cent of the island, as the Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia, which remain British territory and not a base on Cypriot soil. RAF Akrotiri, built on the salt-lake peninsula from 1955, has been the operational point of British and allied air power in the eastern Mediterranean ever since, from Suez in 1956 through Lebanon, Iraq, Libya and Syria. Some 11,000 Cypriots work in the areas, which contain villages, farmland and a wetland of international importance as well as runways and listening aerials.

finds.t: The longest runway on Cyprus, laid out on reclaimed ground beside the salt lake and used within a year for the Suez operation; it is Britain's main air bridge to the Middle East and a NATO reinforcement base.
A signals intelligence station in the Dhekelia area, part of the UKUSA network, whose aerial farms are the reason Cyprus mattered to the Cold War far beyond its size.
The administrative and garrison centre of the western area, seat of the Sovereign Base Areas Administration with its own police, courts and law.

finds.p: Natural; protected in the modern period
finds.t: The largest inland water body on Cyprus, a Ramsar wetland inside a military area where thousands of flamingos winter; the coexistence of bombers and birds has made the base an unlikely conservation manager.

finds.n: Monastery of Saint Nicholas of the Cats
finds.p: Founded by tradition 327 CE; present buildings later
finds.t: A monastery on the peninsula whose cats were said to have been imported to kill snakes; it lies inside the base area and is still occupied by nuns.

The treaty that created the Republic also carved out the two areas as British sovereign territory, with rights of movement and training across the Republic. Cypriot politics has argued about them ever since without changing them; Britain offered to cede about half the land under the 2004 settlement plan.
Greek Cypriots displaced in 1974 were housed at Trachoni and Kolossi inside the Akrotiri area, and the Achna forest settlement grew inside Dhekelia, so the bases hold their own refugee history.

new_settlements.name: Nicosia International Airport
new_settlements.modern: West of Nicosia, inside the UN Protected Area
new_settlements.desc: The island's airport from 1939, first as RAF Nicosia and then as the civil gateway of the colony and the Republic, with a new terminal by the Wiesbaden firm Dorsch und Gehrmann opened on 27 March 1968. It was fought over in July and August 1974, declared a United Nations Protected Area, and has stood derelict ever since, with Cyprus Airways aircraft rotting on the apron. It is now the headquarters of the United Nations force, and the Committee on Missing Persons has its laboratory in the same protected area. Larnaca airport, opened in February 1975, replaced it.

finds.t: A modernist terminal costing about £1.1 million, half a million of it British money, built for a tourist boom that lasted six years; its check-in hall, signage and furniture are still in place under thick dust.
finds.w: In situ, UN Protected Area (no public access)

finds.t: A Cyprus Airways Trident and other airframes were left on the apron when the fighting stopped and have never been moved, the most photographed single image of the island's division.

Turkish aircraft bombed the field on 20 July and Turkish and Greek Cypriot forces fought for it; the United Nations declared it a protected area and required both sides to stay 500 metres back, which is why the buildings survived at all.
The United Nations force runs the island's peacekeeping operation from the old airport site, using the former airport buildings and married quarters as offices and accommodation.

The bicommunal Committee on Missing Persons examines and identifies exhumed remains in a laboratory inside the protected area, where Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot scientists work side by side. It is the one place on the island where the two communities have jointly and continuously handled the evidence of 1963 to 1974.
finds.w: In situ, UN Protected Area, Nicosia

finds.t: The field was laid out in 1939 by Shell and the contractors Pierides and Michaelides, became a Royal Air Force station through the Second World War and the emergency, and shared the runway with civil traffic until the RAF concentrated at Akrotiri.

new_settlements.name: Varosha (Maras)
new_settlements.modern: Southern quarter of Famagusta, fenced since 1974
new_settlements.desc: The Greek suburb outside the walls of Famagusta, where Orthodox Cypriots lived because for much of the Ottoman period they were kept out of the walled city, and which by the early 1970s had become the most modern resort in the eastern Mediterranean, a wall of hotels along a long sand beach that drew Elizabeth Taylor and Brigitte Bardot. Its people fled in August 1974 and the Turkish army fenced the quarter off empty. Security Council resolution 550 of 1984 called for its transfer to United Nations administration and its resettlement by anyone other than its inhabitants inadmissible; part of the beachfront was opened to visitors in October 2020, which the Republic and the Security Council rejected. Forty-five years of sea air have left the buildings beyond saving.

finds.n: The hotel strip on John F. Kennedy Avenue
finds.t: A line of high-rise hotels, the Asterias, Grecian, Argo, King George and others, built in a decade on a sandbar of a beach; their concrete frames still stand with curtains in the windows and lift shafts open to the sky.

The Turkish army closed the quarter with wire, oil drums and painted warnings and kept it sealed for forty-six years, an act without real parallel: a whole modern town held empty as a bargaining counter.

For decades the only way to see Varosha was through binoculars from the Greek Cypriot village of Deryneia on the far side of the buffer zone, where cafes set up telescopes; the viewpoint is itself now a piece of the island's memory industry.

The Council declared attempts to settle any part of Varosha by people other than its inhabitants inadmissible and called for the area to be handed to the United Nations, a position it restated in resolution 789 of 1992 and after the 2020 opening.

A mosque inside the fenced area that held its first prayers in forty-seven years in July 2021, part of the partial reopening; the reopening was condemned by the Security Council as inconsistent with its resolutions.

A beach strip and some streets were opened to visitors, with pavements, cycle hire and viewing platforms among the ruins; several hundred thousand people had walked in by early 2022. Property claims by the original owners are being pursued through the Immovable Property Commission and the European Court of Human Rights.

The quarter's name is simply the Ottoman word for the suburb outside a fortress. Greek Cypriots were largely excluded from living inside Famagusta's walls until the nineteenth century, which is why the Orthodox town grew here and why Varosha, not the walled city, became the modern commercial centre.

new_settlements.name: Kokkina (Erenkoy)
new_settlements.modern: Coastal exclave on Morphou Bay, Nicosia district
new_settlements.desc: A small Turkish Cypriot coastal village in the Tillyria that became the most fought-over point of the 1963 to 1964 crisis, because it was the one beach through which men and weapons could reach the Turkish Cypriot fighters from Turkey. In August 1964 the National Guard under Grivas attacked it with several thousand men; Turkey answered with two days of air strikes using napalm on Kokkina and the surrounding Greek villages, killing more than fifty people including civilians, and a United Nations ceasefire held from 9 August. The enclave was never taken. Its people were moved to Yialousa in 1976 and it is now a closed military area with an annual commemoration.

finds.t: The ridges and the shore where the National Guard's attack was stopped, still marked by trenches and positions; the Turkish Cypriot account calls it the Erenkoy Resistance and it is the founding battle of the modern Turkish Cypriot security narrative.

Turkish Air Force aircraft bombed, strafed and napalmed the area for two days, hitting Greek Cypriot villages, Polis and a hospital; it was the first use of Turkish air power over Cyprus and it forced the ceasefire. The pilot Cengiz Topel was shot down and died in Greek Cypriot hands, and is commemorated in the north.
A tended cemetery inside the exclave holding the Turkish Cypriot dead of the battle, the focus of the yearly ceremony every August.

Small boats from Turkey landed men, arms and food on this shore for the fighters of the TMT, which is exactly why the Republic tried to take it; the pattern of enclaves supplied from outside shaped the whole decade.

Mansoura, Alevga, Pachyammos and their neighbours were caught between the enclave and the attack and were bombed in 1964; several were abandoned in 1974. The whole coast is now thinly populated on both sides of the line.
The inhabitants were moved after 1974 to Yialousa in the Karpas, renamed Yeni Erenkoy, so the name of the village now sits 130 km away from the ground it fought for.

new_settlements.name: Mari naval base and Vasilikos
new_settlements.desc: On 11 July 2011 ninety-eight containers of gunpowder and ammunition, seized in 2009 from the Cypriot-flagged ship Monchegorsk carrying Iranian material towards Syria and then left stacked in the open at the Evangelos Florakis naval base, caught fire and exploded. Thirteen people were killed, including the navy commander, the base commander and six firefighters, and about sixty-two were injured. The blast wrecked the neighbouring Vasilikos power station, which supplied roughly half the island's electricity, and left damage estimated at around two billion euros. An independent inquiry found that President Christofias bore primary responsibility; the defence minister, the foreign minister and the National Guard commander resigned.

finds.n: The crater at the naval base
finds.t: The store site where the containers stood, about 400 metres from the power station and near the village of Mari, whose houses were also damaged. The containers had been left in the open for more than two years despite repeated warnings.

The island's largest thermal station, reduced to a shell by the blast; rolling power cuts followed through the summer of 2011 and electricity had to be bought in and generators leased. It has since been repaired and expanded.

Artillery propellant, shell components and primers taken off a Russian-owned, Cypriot-flagged ship intercepted in the Red Sea under United Nations sanctions on Iran; a sanctions success became a domestic disaster because nobody would take responsibility for destroying the material.

A one-man independent investigation concluded that the president bore primary responsibility for the failure to move or destroy the cargo. The report is one of the sharpest documents of official accountability in the Republic's history.
A monument and annual commemoration for the dead, most of them firefighters and sailors who went towards the fire; the fire service's losses reshaped Cypriot civil-defence doctrine.

The stretch from Zygi to Vasilikos carries the power station, a cement works and the terminal planned for imported natural gas, the Republic's answer to having lost its northern infrastructure in 1974.

new_settlements.name: Ayia Napa
new_settlements.desc: A Venetian-period monastery beside a spring, a fishing and farming hamlet of a few hundred people until the 1970s, and then the place where the Republic rebuilt the tourist industry it lost with Varosha and Kyrenia in 1974. It now has more than 175 hotels and apartment blocks and a bed capacity of about 27,000, took over 700,000 visitors in 2017 and became a fixture of the British club circuit at the turn of the century. Nothing shows the economic shape of the post-1974 Republic more plainly: hotels on the south-east coast paid for by refugees and by state loan guarantees.

finds.t: A walled monastery around a sunken cave church beside a spring, built by the Venetians about 1500 with older Byzantine wall sections; it functioned into the Ottoman period, then as a parish church, and is now a museum and a chapel used by several denominations.

finds.n: The monastery's octagonal fountain and sycamore
finds.p: 16th century; tree said to be 600 years old
finds.t: A domed marble fountain house in the courtyard fed by the spring that made the site, shaded by a huge sycamore fig; the spring is why a monastery stood on a waterless coast.

The sandbar and islet that made the resort's name; it topped a TripAdvisor list of European beaches in 2011, and its beach bars were the centre of the garage and dance scene that drew British visitors between about 1999 and 2003.
A museum of the sea holding a full-scale reconstruction of the Kyrenia ship, the Kyrenia II, alongside marine and archaeological collections, built to give the resort something to do in winter.

The small harbour and its remaining boats, the whole of the village economy before tourism; local memory of the change from fishing to hotels within one generation is well recorded in oral history projects.

finds.n: The sea caves and the Cape Greco park
finds.t: Wave-cut caves and arches in the limestone east of the town, within a national forest park that was left undeveloped as the hotels spread, a rare planning restraint on this coast.
The original church cut into the rock below present ground level, reached down a flight of steps, with the spring beside it; the whole monastery is arranged around this hole in the ground.
A domed marble fountain house in the courtyard carrying carved heads and a boar's head spout, the best piece of secular Venetian carving on the island.
Two-storey ranges of vaulted cells and a refectory around a walled court entered by a gate under a bell tower, Italian in proportion and Cypriot in stone.
A vast Ficus sycomorus outside the south wall, said to be as old as the monastery and one of the oldest trees on Cyprus.

finds.n: Latin and Orthodox side by side
finds.t: A Latin chapel adjoining the Orthodox cave church, the physical form of the compromise the two communities had reached by the end of Venetian rule; the house was deserted in the seventeenth century and the church later served the Greek village.

new_settlements.name: The Kokkinochoria and the water problem
new_settlements.modern: Xylofagou, Liopetri, Frenaros, Avgorou and their neighbours
new_settlements.desc: The red villages of the south-east, named for the terra rossa soil that makes their potatoes, are the clearest case of the island's central modern problem: there is not enough water. From the 1950s cheap diesel pumps and boreholes let the Kokkinochoria grow two or three potato crops a year for the British market, until over-pumping drew seawater into the aquifer and salted the wells. Cyprus answered with dams, then with desalination, and in the drought of 2008 with tankers of drinking water from Greece. The 1974 line also runs along the top of the district, cutting these villages off from Famagusta, their market town.

finds.t: Deep red iron-rich soils over limestone, worked in tiny plots and irrigated from boreholes, giving two and sometimes three crops a year; the new potato became one of the Republic's largest agricultural exports, most of it to Britain.

Thousands of private wells drew the water table below sea level and salt water moved inland, ruining wells that had been sweet within living memory. The Kokkinochoria aquifer is the standard Cypriot example of a groundwater body pumped past recovery.
finds.w: In situ; Water Development Department records

finds.t: The Republic built more than a hundred dams and reservoirs, among them Achna in the east and the great Kouris dam in the south, and laid the Southern Conveyor to move water along the coast; storage still depends entirely on how much it rains.
Reverse-osmosis plants at Dhekelia, near Larnaca and later in the west now supply most of the drinking water of the government-controlled area, turning a rainfall problem into an electricity problem.
finds.w: In situ, Dhekelia and Larnaca district

finds.t: After successive dry winters the Republic chartered tankers to bring drinking water from Greece, an episode that did more than any report to make water politics visible to the public.

Famagusta was the natural port and market of these villages; after 1974 the buffer zone ran between them and it, and the district's produce went instead to Limassol and Larnaca. Fields on the far side of the line have been out of use for fifty years.
finds.w: In situ, along the buffer zone

finds.t: The Augustinian church of Saint Mary, wrecked in the siege, was converted by Lala Mustafa Pasha in 1571 in the belief that the Caliph Omar had rested on the spot; Lusignan tomb slabs are reused in its floor. The hamam of the same complex was restored in 2002 to 2004 under the Nicosia Master Plan, still works as a bath house, and won the top Europa Nostra conservation prize in 2006.

The sandstone mansion of the dragoman, the Greek interpreter and tax intermediary who was the richest and most hated man on the island, built round a courtyard with its own three-room hamam. Kornesios was executed at Constantinople in 1809. Saved from demolition in the 1950s, opened as a museum in 1960 and given a Europa Nostra award in 1988, it is the best surviving picture of how power actually worked in late Ottoman Cyprus.

The Ottoman authorities gave a ruined Byzantine and Gothic church beside Selimiye to the Haramayn foundation in 1573 for use as a covered cloth market; it fell out of use when the municipal covered market, the Bandabuliya, opened in 1932 next door. The two buildings, forty metres and 360 years apart, are the Ottoman and the colonial versions of the same function.

finds.n: Faneromeni church and the Marble Mausoleum
finds.t: The largest church of the walled city, rebuilt in 1872 on the site of an older convent, with a marble mausoleum to its east holding the relics of Archbishop Kyprianos, the three bishops and the clergy executed by the Ottoman authorities on 9 July 1821. Faneromeni School opposite is one of the oldest on the island.

Founded by Archbishop Kyprianos as the Hellenic School, on a site that had held a school since 1753, and reorganised as the Pancyprian Gymnasium in 1893; the present neoclassical building followed a fire in 1920. Its pupils include Makarios III, Glafcos Clerides, Tassos Papadopoulos, Georgios Grivas and the Nobel economist Christopher Pissarides, and its classrooms were a nursery of both enosis and the 1931 and 1955 movements.

finds.n: Government House, now the Presidential Palace
finds.t: The first Government House was a prefabricated building shipped from England in 1878, intended for Ceylon and carried up from the coast by camel. A crowd of about 5,000 burned it on 21 October 1931 and the cost was charged back to the population; Maurice Webb designed the sandstone replacement, built between 1932 and 1937 for £70,000. It became the Presidential Palace in 1960, was burned again in the coup of July 1974 and was rebuilt in 1977 with Greek money.

Thirteen graves in the yard of the Central Prison holding the men the British hanged during the emergency, among them Michalakis Karaolis and Andreas Demetriou on 10 May 1956 and the eighteen-year-old Evagoras Pallikaridis on 14 March 1957, together with fighters killed in action including Markos Drakos, Grigoris Afxentiou, Stylianos Lenas and Kyriakos Matsis. The gallows and cells are shown as a national monument.

finds.n: The Green Line through the city
finds.t: Major-General Peter Young drew the ceasefire line across Nicosia with a green chinagraph pencil on a map on 30 December 1963; the buffer zone it became runs 180 km across the island and covers 346 square kilometres, from twenty metres wide in the old city to seven kilometres in the plain. Nicosia has been the last divided capital in Europe since 1974. The Ledra Palace hotel, opened in 1949 and shell-scarred in 1974, has served as the United Nations barracks, and the crossing beside it was the first to open, in April 2003, followed by the pedestrian crossing on Ledra Street in the old city in 2008.

A plaque over the entrance dates the Ottoman rebuilding of the fort to 1625, though a Turkish garrison had held the site since 1570 and there was a Lusignan work here before that. It carried the guns that saluted arriving consuls, then served the British as a prison with a gallows into the 1940s, and is now the Larnaca Medieval Museum.

Built over the tomb found in 890 inscribed 'Lazarus, four days dead, friend of Christ'. Taken as a mosque after 1571 and sold back to the Orthodox in 1589, it was then shared with Latin worshippers for about two centuries, an arrangement recorded in Latin graffiti in the walls. Its bell tower went up after the Ottoman reform of 1857 permitted belfries. A fire in 1970 destroyed much of the iconostasis, and in November 1972 human remains were found in a marble sarcophagus under the altar and identified as part of the saint's relics.

The Ottoman authorities required European consuls to live at Larnaca, and the town became the island's window on the world: French, Venetian, British, Russian and Swedish consulates, dragomans, merchants and the antiquities dealers who shipped much of Cypriot archaeology abroad. Cotton, carobs, salt, silk and wine went out through the roadstead by lighter because there was no harbour.

finds.n: The salt lake and the salt trade
finds.t: Salt raked from the lake beside the town was one of Cyprus's steadiest exports under Venetian, Ottoman and British rule; commercial harvesting stopped in the 1980s, and the lake is now protected for its wintering flamingos.

Thrown up in a few months on the edge of the salt lake after Nicosia airport was lost, initially with a converted cargo shed for a terminal; it became the Republic's main gateway and got a new terminal in 2009.

The town absorbed thousands of displaced people, took over the trade of Famagusta with a new commercial port, and grew a marina and a seafront palm promenade; the Turkish Cypriot quarter around the fort emptied in 1975. Modern Larnaca is a 1974 city as much as an ancient one.

After the siege the Ottoman authorities settled the walled city with Muslims and largely excluded Orthodox Cypriots from living inside it, which is why the Greek town grew as Varosha outside the gates. Travellers through the eighteenth century describe a garrison town of a few hundred people among two dozen ruined churches.

Cafer Pasha brought water into the walled city and built a domed bath house and a street fountain, the main Ottoman civic works in Famagusta; the fountain still stands near the cathedral square and the bath survives in part.

finds.n: Famagusta harbour and the railway terminus
finds.t: The British dredged and walled the silted harbour and made it the colony's main port, with the Cyprus Government Railway running from the quay to Nicosia from 21 October 1905. Locomotive No. 1 is preserved at the station.

The Republic declared Famagusta a closed port after 1974, so the busiest harbour on the island trades only with Turkey; the resulting legal argument about direct trade with the north has run through the European courts for decades.

The citadel was consolidated and reopened by the bicommunal Technical Committee on Cultural Heritage with United Nations and European Union funding, the most visible product of the one negotiating track that has kept working through every political freeze.

finds.n: The Grand Mosque and the Turkish quarter
finds.t: Djami Kebir, the Great Mosque, stands with its bath house a few steps from the castle in what was the Turkish Cypriot quarter of the old town; the quarter emptied in 1975 and its lanes are now bars and workshops. Limassol was a town where the two communities lived most closely mixed.

Stone warehouses on the shore beside the castle where carob pods, the black gold of Cyprus, were stored and shipped; the complex is now a museum, cinema and restaurant quarter. Carobs were among the colony's top three exports for decades.

Limassol became the island's wine town: ETKO dates its founding to 1844 and KEO was set up in 1927, with SODAP and LOEL following, all drawing grapes from the Troodos foothills. The Limassol Wine Festival has run since 1961.

A deep-water harbour finished just before the war, which then had to carry almost all the Republic's trade after Famagusta was lost; it remains the island's main port and a Mediterranean transhipment stop.

Limassol took the largest share of the displaced, and whole quarters of the eastern suburbs began as government refugee estates of identical low houses; the city's population roughly doubled in a decade and it overtook Famagusta as the island's commercial capital.

A marina and residential development beside the old town opened in 2014, followed by a line of high-rise towers along the seafront built partly on investment-for-citizenship money; the most conspicuous physical result of the post-2013 recovery.
The oldest Ottoman building in the town, a small stone mosque with a squat minaret and a fountain, built for the garrison a decade after the conquest, just above the old harbour.

finds.n: The castle as a colonial prison
finds.t: The British used the Venetian fortress as a prison and, during the 1955 to 1959 emergency, as a detention centre for EOKA suspects; the cells and the exercise yards are shown to visitors alongside the medieval work.

Turkish forces came ashore on Five Mile Beach west of Kyrenia at dawn on 20 July 1974 and pushed inland to link with the Turkish Cypriot enclave in Nicosia. A monument and a museum now stand at the landing point, and the anniversary is a public holiday in the north.

finds.n: Bitter Lemons and the house at Bellapais
finds.t: Lawrence Durrell bought a house in Bellapais, taught in Nicosia and worked for the colonial information service, and wrote Bitter Lemons about watching the island slide into the emergency; the book shaped how a generation of British readers understood Cyprus, and the house is still pointed out.

finds.n: The harbour and the tourist town
finds.t: The horseshoe harbour with its carob warehouses converted to restaurants was the postcard image of Cyprus before 1974 and is now the tourist centre of the north, ringed by hotels and casinos serving visitors from Turkey.

Three large stones, two upright and one laid across them, cover the grave of Umm Haram bint Milhan, a kinswoman of the Prophet's foster-mother who is said to have fallen from her mule and died during the Arab raid of 649. Local tradition holds that the top stone hung unsupported in the air; the shrine was venerated by Ottoman sailors, who saluted it from the sea.

The mosque and minaret beside the tomb were built under the governor Seyyid Mehmed Emin, completing a complex whose tomb chamber and enclosure had been raised from about 1760; the inscription over the door records the work. It is among the most important Muslim monuments on the island.

finds.n: The takke's garden and dervish lodge
finds.t: Cells, a fountain, cypresses and palms around the mosque, laid out as a lodge for the dervishes and pilgrims who kept the shrine; the tekke held property in the district endowed for its upkeep.

finds.n: The salt lake and its flamingos
finds.t: The lake that once salted Larnaca's export trade now fills and dries each year and holds thousands of greater flamingos in winter; it is a Natura 2000 site and the setting that makes the tekke's silhouette famous.

The tekke lies in the government-controlled area but is maintained for Muslim worship, and access for Turkish Cypriots to pray here has been one of the small confidence-building measures negotiated since the crossings opened in 2003.

finds.n: Throni and the tomb of Makarios III
finds.t: The first president of the Republic, who began here as a novice in 1926, was buried on 3 August 1977 on the hilltop of Throni above the monastery at his own wish; a shrine to the Virgin stands beside the grave and the site draws pilgrims and tourists in equal numbers.

Kykkos was caught in the reprisals of 1821: its abbot was among those put to death and the monastery's property was seized, a reminder that the richest Orthodox house on the island held its wealth entirely at the sultan's pleasure.

Kykkos ran dependencies, farms and urban properties across Cyprus and beyond, and the income paid for village schools, scholarships and the printing of books; monastic estates were the main Greek Cypriot institution that survived the Ottoman centuries intact.

The Kykkos and Machairas forests sheltered EOKA groups and their caches, and the monastery is widely held to have helped them; British forces mounted repeated searches in the area. The monastery museum and the nearby memorials present the campaign from the Greek Cypriot side.

In drought the icon of the Panagia Kykkotissa was carried out of the mountains in procession to the parched villages, a practice recorded from the Ottoman centuries into living memory, and one of the clearest links between the island's religion and its water.

finds.n: The estate as an Ottoman chiftlik
finds.t: After 1570 the commandery's lands passed into Ottoman hands as a farm estate whose revenues went to state and pious foundations, and the keep became a store and a farmhouse. The sugar industry it had been built for was already dead, undercut by Atlantic and Madeiran sugar.

finds.n: The labour of the sugar works
finds.t: The cane fields and refinery were worked by a mixed force of Cypriot serfs, Syrian and Arab labourers and slaves, and the mill was driven by water brought by the aqueduct; the documentary record of this workforce is one of the fuller pictures of medieval Mediterranean plantation labour.

The Department of Antiquities took the castle in hand in the colonial period, cleared and consolidated the keep and the mill and opened them; the flat roof and its view over the Akrotiri plain date from that work.

The sweet wine named for the knights' commandery is now a protected designation of origin made in fourteen named villages above Limassol from sun-dried xynisteri and mavro grapes; the claim that it is the oldest named wine still in production rests on the medieval documents rather than on continuity of practice.

The village sits on the edge of the Akrotiri Sovereign Base Area, and part of its land was used to house Greek Cypriots displaced in 1974, so a Hospitaller estate now shares its fields with British sovereign territory and a refugee estate.

The Venetians blew up the Lusignan harbour forts in 1570; the Ottomans rebuilt one tower with a vaulted hall and prison cells in 1592, and the British used it as a salt store before it was scheduled as an ancient monument in 1935. It is the working emblem of Paphos harbour.

Paphos was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1980 for the whole ensemble from Palaepaphos to the Tombs of the Kings and the Roman houses, one of the first sites listed for Cyprus and the reason the archaeological park was consolidated.

A destructive earthquake in the Paphos district killed dozens of people and wrecked villages and churches across the west; much of the district's plain vernacular architecture was rebuilt afterwards in concrete, which is why so little old fabric survives outside the hill villages.

The Turkish Cypriot quarter of upper Paphos, with its mosque and bath, emptied when its people moved north in 1975 and was allocated to Greek Cypriots displaced from the north; two displacements are stacked in the same streets.

An airport opened at Paphos in 1983 turned the quietest district of the Republic into a tourist and retirement coast, and Paphos was European Capital of Culture in 2017, which paid for the excavation and display of much of the old town.

A monastery on the shore beside ancient Lambousa, with a domed church of Byzantine and Gothic phases, whose name means 'made without hands'. It stands inside a Turkish military area and has been inaccessible and largely unmaintained since 1974.

Lapithos was the island's best-known pottery town, turning out glazed and slip-decorated earthenware jugs, bowls and storage jars on the wheel; museum collections of Cypriot folk pottery are largely Lapithos work, and the craft died with the displacement of 1974.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum and Folk Art Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: Springs on the Kyrenia range fed terraced gardens of lemons, mulberries for silk and vegetables, made the town unusually prosperous and gave it a reputation for water in a dry island; the channels and washing places survive in the lanes.

Lapithos's Greek Cypriot population, several thousand strong, fled or was expelled in 1974 and now lives scattered in the south; the town, renamed Lapta, was settled by Turkish Cypriots from the south and by families from Turkey and is today a tourist village. Both displacements are documented village by village in the PRIO displacement project.
finds.w: In situ, Lapta; PRIO Cyprus Displacement Centre

events: The Latin cathedrals of Nicosia and Famagusta become the Selimiye and Lala Mustafa Pasha mosques; the first Friday prayer in Nicosia is held on 15 September 1570
A ruined church beside Selimiye is granted to the Haramayn foundation as the Bedesten, the covered cloth market
A Tuscan squadron raids Famagusta, the last western attempt on the island
The fort at Larnaca is rebuilt; Larnaca becomes the port of trade and the seat of the European consuls
Boyacioglu Mehmed Agha leads a revolt of local aghas that holds the island for about two years
Cyprus is granted as an arpalik to the Grand Vizier and run by a muhassil who farms its taxes
Ebubekir Pasha begins the aqueduct that will carry water about ten kilometres to Larnaca; it serves the town until 1939
The dragoman Hadjigeorgakis Kornesios builds his Nicosia mansion; the dragomans are the richest men on the island
Muslim townsmen and peasants riot in Nicosia against the tax power of the archbishop and the dragoman
Hadjigeorgakis Kornesios is executed at Constantinople and his property seized
Archbishop Kyprianos founds the Hellenic School of Nicosia, later the Pancyprian Gymnasium
The three bishops are beheaded and Archbishop Kyprianos hanged in Nicosia on 9 July; executions and confiscations follow for months, and Kykkos loses its abbot and its lands
The Tanzimat reforms make Cyprus a sanjak under a mutasarrif; the Ottoman land code of 1858 follows
Ottoman reform permits Christians to build bell towers; the belfry of Ayios Lazaros rises at Larnaca
The Cyprus Convention is signed on 4 June; the British flag is raised at Nicosia on 12 July by Lord John Hay and Wolseley lands at Larnaca on 22 July
A summer hill station is laid out on the Troodos; the governor's cottage is begun at 1,700 metres
The Cyprus Government Railway opens from Famagusta to Nicosia on 21 October; it reaches Morphou in 1907 and Evrychou in 1915
Intercommunal rioting in Limassol and Nicosia, the first serious violence between the two communities under British rule
The Cyprus Mines Corporation is founded and reopens the ancient copper of Skouriotissa; Mavrovouni follows in 1929
The Treaty of Lausanne confirms British sovereignty; Turkish Cypriots are given two years to opt for Turkish nationality and thousands emigrate
The Cyprus Tribute is abolished; since 1878 Cyprus had paid about £92,800 a year of its revenues towards defaulted Ottoman loans
Seven demonstrators are killed, more than 2,600 arrested and ten leaders exiled after the October riots
About 30,000 Cypriots serve in the Cyprus Regiment and other units during the Second World War
Britain offers a Consultative Assembly and a constitution; the Greek Cypriot leadership boycotts it and the offer lapses in 1948
Long strikes in the copper mines and a growing left-wing labour movement under the Pancyprian Federation of Labour
A church-organised plebiscite records about 96 per cent for union with Greece; Makarios III is elected archbishop
A state of emergency is declared; the Turkish Resistance Organisation is founded in answer to EOKA and presses for partition
Makarios is deported to the Seychelles in March; nine men are hanged at Nicosia Central Prison between May 1956 and March 1957
Grigoris Afxentiou is burned out of his hideout at Machairas on 3 March
Four EOKA men die in the barn at Liopetri on 2 September; the Macmillan plan is rejected by both communities
Grivas declares a ceasefire on 9 March; the emergency has cost about 500 lives, including 156 British servicemen and police
Britain retains 254 square kilometres as the Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia, about three per cent of the island
Cyprus joins the Commonwealth and, in 1961, the Non-Aligned Movement
Major-General Peter Young draws the ceasefire line across Nicosia with a green chinagraph pencil on 30 December
Fighting at Kokkina in August; Turkish aircraft napalm the Tillyria villages and a UN ceasefire follows on 9 August
Fighting at Kophinou and Ayios Theodoros brings Greece and Turkey close to war
About 160,000 Greek Cypriots are displaced south and some 45,000 to 60,000 Turkish Cypriots move north; Turkey holds 36 per cent of the island
Larnaca airport opens in February; Nicosia's stays sealed inside the UN Protected Area
Makarios dies in August; the high-level agreement of that year accepts a bizonal federation in principle
Security Council resolution 550 declares any resettlement of Varosha by others than its inhabitants inadmissible
The first large desalination plant opens at Dhekelia; the island begins to drink the sea
The Ledra Palace crossing opens on 23 April and hundreds of thousands cross in the first months

The Annan plan is rejected by about 76 per cent of Greek Cypriots and accepted by about 65 per cent of Turkish Cypriots on 24 April; Cyprus joins the EU on 1 May with the acquis suspended in the north
Drought forces the Republic to ship drinking water from Greece by tanker
An ammunition store explodes at the Mari naval base on 11 July, killing thirteen and wrecking the Vasilikos power station
A ten-billion-euro bailout in March closes Laiki Bank and imposes losses on deposits over 100,000 euros
Reunification talks collapse at Crans-Montana in July after the closest approach to a settlement since 2004
Part of the Varosha beachfront is opened to visitors, drawing Security Council condemnation
Of 2,002 people listed as missing from 1963 to 1974, about 1,080 have been identified and returned to their families

rulers.t: Commander of the conquest and the island's first governor; he had Bragadin flayed at Famagusta and gave his name to its cathedral-mosque.
First beylerbeyi of the new province of Cyprus, credited with building the Buyuk Han in Nicosia; some scholars give the han to his successor Sinan Pasha.
Cyprus was a full eyalet under a governor of pasha rank with sanjaks on the mainland; some seventy governors came and went, few staying more than two years.
The island was downgraded to a sanjak assigned to the Ottoman admiral, who sent a deputy; real power passed to local aghas and tax farmers, and revolts followed.

rulers.n: The muhassils of the Grand Vizier
rulers.t: Cyprus was granted to the Grand Vizier as a source of income and run by a muhassil who bought the right to collect its taxes, the arrangement that made both extortion and the Church's power possible.
Governor of the brief restored eyalet, remembered for good order and for beginning the aqueduct to Larnaca in 1747.
Muhassil who doubled the tax demand; Greeks and Turks together stormed the palace in Nicosia and killed him, one of the few joint risings of the period.
Muhassil who ordered the hanging of Archbishop Kyprianos and the beheading of the three bishops on 9 July 1821 and the executions and confiscations that followed.

After the Tanzimat reforms Cyprus was governed by a mutasarrif under the Archipelago province and then, from 1861 and again from 1870, as a separate mutasarrifate until the British took over the administration.
Archbishop under whom the Porte came to treat the prelates as spokesmen of the Orthodox flock, the step conventionally dated to 1660.
Consolidated the archbishop's standing as head of the Greek community, with the right to petition Constantinople over the governor's head.
Presided over the years when the archbishop and the four bishops collected the Christians' taxes and were, in practice, the island's civil government.
Interpreter to the governor and tax intermediary, the richest man on the island; executed at Constantinople in 1809 after complaints from both communities.
Founder of the Hellenic School of Nicosia in 1812; hanged from a tree outside the palace on 9 July 1821 in the reprisals for the Greek revolt.
Raised the British flag at Nicosia on 12 July 1878 and held the administration for ten days.
First High Commissioner, who landed at Larnaca on 22 July 1878 and set up the administration under canvas.
Built the first roads, courts and schools and the summer residence on the Troodos; the longest-serving of the early administrators.
Presided over the first stirrings of organised enosis politics in the Legislative Council.
High Commissioner during years of locust campaigns, agricultural debt and emigration.
Faced deadlock in the Legislative Council between Greek and Turkish members and the British bloc.
Opened the Cyprus Government Railway in 1905 and the rebuilt harbour at Famagusta.
In office when Britain annexed Cyprus in November 1914 after the Ottoman entry into the war.
Administered the island through the war, when Britain offered Cyprus to Greece and Athens declined.
Last High Commissioner and first Governor when Cyprus became a Crown Colony in 1925.
Aesthete and orientalist whose Government House, and his own library, were burned in the riots of October 1931.
Held the governorship for a year in the immediate repression after the riots.
Governor of the authoritarian 'Palmerocracy', with the Legislative Council and municipal elections abolished, the press censored and the flying of Greek flags banned.
Relaxed some of Palmer's restrictions as war began and raised the Cyprus Regiment.
Governor through the war years, when trade unions and communal politics revived.
Offered a Consultative Assembly and a constitution which the Greek Cypriot leadership boycotted; resigned when the offer failed.
In office for the 1950 enosis plebiscite and the election of Makarios III as archbishop.
Governor when the constitution was again refused and EOKA opened its campaign on 1 April 1955.
Soldier-governor of the emergency, who declared a state of emergency, deported Makarios to the Seychelles and authorised the hangings.
Last Governor, who wound the emergency down and handed over power at independence on 16 August 1960.
