Two coordinates are deliberately approximate and I have said so rather than guess to three real decimals. Pano Lefkara: the only figures I could verify are given to the arcminute (34 deg 52 min N, 33 deg 18 min E), so 34.867/33.303 is the village centre to about 500 m. Troodos: no source gives coordinates for the Presidential Cottage itself, so I have used the Troodos community point 34.922/32.880 and framed the entry as the hill station rather than the single house; the cottage is roughly 1 km from that point.

Kokkinochoria is a district, not a point. I anchored it between Xylofagou and Liopetri at 34.977/33.850. If you would rather not have a regional dot, the water material could be folded into the era_events for republic and one find under kition.

I did NOT create separate settlements for Buyuk Han, the Selimiye or Lala Mustafa Pasha mosques, the Omeriye complex, the Arab Ahmet quarter, the covered market, Faneromeni, the Pancyprian Gymnasium, the Cyprus Museum, the Central Prison, Government House or the Ledra Palace, because all of them lie within 2 km of the existing nicosia or famagusta dots and would clutter the map. They are in extra_finds instead. That is why the nicosia list has eight finds rather than the suggested three to six; trim the last two if you want it shorter.

Larnaca has no settlement of its own here because the existing kition entry sits at 33.63/34.92, which is the same ground, and its range already runs to 2026. I therefore added Larnaca's Ottoman, British and modern material as extra_finds on kition, which was not on your list; drop it if kition is spoken for by another agent. The Bekir Pasha aqueduct is 3.3 km west of that dot and is given its own entry.

Overlap risk with other agents. Peristerona's church is 9th or 10th century and may belong to a Byzantine brief; I have written the entry around the church-and-mosque pairing and the mixed village so it earns its place in the Ottoman era. Machairas and Chrysorrogiatissa were founded in the 12th century but everything visible is 18th and 19th century. Fikardou and Machairas are only 2.7 km apart, which is real geography, not an error. Kolossi's existing range ends at 1570; if you take the Ottoman and modern finds I have proposed for it, extend the range to 2026.

The 1660 recognition of the archbishop. Your era text flags this as popular history and it deserves the flag. Cypriot scholarship generally has the Porte accept the archbishop and bishops as spokesmen (kocabasi) of the Orthodox in 1660, but the Ottoman Cyprus literature also describes the role as crystallising after 1670, once the island passed to the Kapudan Pasha and local aghas, and as only formalised in 1754 when the prelates became the tax intermediaries. I have kept 1660 out of my new events and put the process in the rulers notes for Nikiforos and Philotheos instead. Treat any single-year date as a convention.

The tribute. The Convention fixed it at £92,799 11s 3d a year, and it was never paid to the Ottomans: it went into the Bank of England to service defaulted Ottoman Crimean War loans guaranteed by Britain and France. Britain abrogated the Convention on 5 November 1914 but kept charging Cypriot revenues; the charge was lifted in 1927, when Britain raised the grant-in-aid to cover it on condition that Cyprus pay £10,000 a year towards imperial defence. Diana Markides's book on the Cyprus Tribute is the authority if you want to go further.

1821. I have used 9 July 1821 for the hanging of Archbishop Kyprianos and the beheading of the bishops Chrysanthos of Paphos, Meletios of Kition and Lavrentios of Kyrenia, with further executions over the following weeks. The English Wikipedia article on Ottoman Cyprus gives 15 October 1821 and a figure of an archbishop, five bishops and thirty-six clergy; other popular sources say 486 executed in the square. The date and the totals are both unreliable in the popular literature. Cyprus has only four bishops plus the archbishop, which is one reason to distrust the 'five bishops' version.

1974 figures are contested and I have used ranges. Displacement: 140,000 to 170,000 Greek Cypriots from the north (the Republic's own figure is about 162,000 to 165,000) and 45,000 to 60,000 Turkish Cypriots from the south, most of that movement in 1975 under the Vienna agreement rather than during the fighting itself. Deaths: roughly 4,500 to 6,000 on the Greek Cypriot and Greek side including about 270 to 1,500 civilians, and about 570 Turkish military dead plus Turkish Cypriot fighters and civilians; the totals are not agreed and no impartial full count exists. Turkey holds 36.2 per cent of the island. Missing: the Committee on Missing Persons works to an agreed list of 1,510 Greek Cypriots and 492 Turkish Cypriots, 2,002 in all, covering both 1963 to 1964 and 1974.

Missing persons, current. As of mid-2026 the CMP had exhumed 1,719 of the 2,002 and identified and returned about 1,081, of whom roughly 764 Greek Cypriots and 311 Turkish Cypriots. These figures move every few weeks; the CMP website carries the current ones. I put the round figure in the 2026 era event on purpose.

Items I checked and dropped as too thin or unverifiable. The monastery of Ayios Panteleimon at Myrtou: I could not verify a date or a coordinate for it, only that it lies near Myrtou (35.308/33.074) and has been in a military area since 1974. Panagia Chrysospiliotissa at Kato Deftera: a rock-cut cave church, but its interest is Byzantine and I could not verify the coordinate. 'Filiko Ergastiri': I could find no reliable account of this and have left it out entirely rather than invent one; if you mean a specific EOKA workshop in Nicosia, please point me at a source. Stavrovouni (34.886/33.436, verified) is a genuine candidate for an Ottoman and British entry since its buildings are almost all 19th century, but its foundation legend belongs to a Byzantine brief, so I left it for whoever has that era.

Single-source or otherwise shaky details in the text above, all flagged here rather than smoothed over: the Cafer Pasha fountain and baths at Famagusta dated 1597; the Aga Cafer Pasha mosque at Kyrenia dated 1580; the date of the Peristerona mosque, which I could not find published; ETKO's claimed founding in 1844 and KEO's in 1927; the opening of the new Limassol port in 1973 to 1974; the Dhekelia desalination plant in 1997; the end of commercial salt harvesting at Larnaca in the 1980s; the 1930s consolidation of Kolossi; the 1592 Ottoman rebuilding of Paphos castle under Ahmed Pasha; the casualty count for the 1953 Paphos earthquake; the figure of about 30,000 Cypriots in the Second World War forces; the number of Turkish Cypriots who emigrated after Lausanne in 1923; the 1912 Limassol riots; the 1804 Nicosia riot; the execution of the abbot of Kykkos in 1821; and Kykkos's role as an EOKA shelter, which is universally asserted in Greek Cypriot sources and not documented in British ones.

The Cyprus Mines Corporation article claims exports of 'nearly a million tons of copper a year' by 1955. That cannot be right for copper metal; it will be ore or concentrate and pyrite. I have avoided any tonnage figure in the Skouriotissa entry for that reason.

The britain rulers list is complete and supersedes the five you have. It includes acting High Commissioner Lord John Hay for the ten days in July 1878 because he, not Wolseley, raised the flag at Nicosia. Malcolm Stevenson appears once, spanning High Commissioner and Governor, since he held both. Short acting appointments between governors are omitted. That gives twenty entries.

For the ottoman power I have given the governing structure rather than a list of names, because Ottoman Cyprus had roughly seventy governors in the first century alone, most of them in post for a year or two and poorly attested in accessible sources, and because the men who actually governed the Greek majority were the archbishop, the bishops and the dragoman. So the list mixes five structural entries (beylerbeyis, mutesellims, muhassils, mutasarrifs) with the four governors who left a mark (Lala Mustafa, Muzaffer, Ebubekir, Cil Osman, Kucuk Mehmed) and four Orthodox figures (Nikiforos, Philotheos, Chrysanthos, Kyprianos) plus the dragoman Kornesios. If you would rather keep 'rulers' strictly to Ottoman officials, delete the last five entries; the structural ones alone still tell the story.

Enosis and taksim. The 1950 plebiscite figure of about 96 per cent is the Church's own count, taken in churches on 15 and 22 January 1950 with an open signature list and, by several accounts, the threat of excommunication for refusing; it is evidence of the Church's mobilising power as much as of opinion. Taksim as an organised Turkish Cypriot demand dates from the mid-1950s, in answer to EOKA, and TMT was founded with Turkish support in 1957 to 1958.

UNESCO listings that belong to existing entries and which I have not duplicated: Paphos, inscribed 1980 (added as a find under neapaphos); Choirokoitia, inscribed 1998 (belongs under khirokitia); the Painted Churches of the Troodos, inscribed 1985 and extended 2001 (belongs under troodos_churches). Lefkara lace was inscribed on the intangible heritage list in 2009 and is in the new lefkara entry. I did not cite a UNESCO URL for it because I could not verify the element's exact permalink and the brief forbids invented URLs.
